sources.evidenceText: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.” On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X. Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. sources.evidenceText: Sunday’s strike on King Khalid International airport kills a Pakistani national. A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority. The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care. The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13. Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way. A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave. The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA. The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s. The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis. The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim. There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

sources.title: Houthi attacks: Eight flights on Dhaka-Riyadh route disrupted, 2,951 passengers affected
sources.evidenceText: Eight flights on the Dhaka-Riyadh route have been disrupted after King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia closed following attacks allegedly by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saturday, affecting 2,951 passengers, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (Caab). Of the affected flights, three were operated by Saudia Airlines, two each by Biman Bangladesh Airlines and Riyadh Air, and one by US-Bangla Airlines, according to the Flight Management System, civil aviation officials said today (11 October). At least 12 people, including two Bangladeshis and four Saudi nationals, were killed and over 300 were injured in the attacks allegedly carried out by the Houthis on the Saudi airport on Saturday afternoon. The airport authorities extended the suspension of operations until 9pm UTC today, equivalent to 3am Bangladesh time today. With no visible progress towards reopening the airport, Biman Bangladesh Airlines has suspended its scheduled flights BG339 and BG340 on the Dhaka-Riyadh and Riyadh-Dhaka routes for 11 and 12 October. The airline said it would inform passengers about the revised flight schedule at noon on Monday, Bangladesh time. Biman also apologised for the temporary inconvenience caused by the suspensions and sought passengers' cooperation. The disruption has affected both Bangladeshi and foreign airlines operating services to and from Riyadh. Authorities are monitoring the situation, while passengers await updates on the resumption of flights and alternative travel arrangements. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam today confirmed that two Bangladeshis were killed and four others were receiving treatment in intensive care units (ICUs) following the attack. The deceased are Md Shahed Ahmed, son of Md Rafiqul Islam, who hailed from Madla village in Shahjahanpur upazila of Bogura, and Md Nasrullah Badrupuri, son of Mawlana Mohammad Ullah, a resident of Badrupur village in Nangalkot upazila of Cumilla. Bangladesh has already lost 14 nationals in ongoing Middle East conflicts, the state minister said, expressing concern over further casualties among Bangladeshi migrant workers. The government will bear the costs of bringing the bodies of the deceased Bangladeshis back home, she said at the ministry today. Various nations, including the United States, have condemned the incidents. US President Donald Trump indicated that he was considering whether his country should join the war against the Houthis. Arab and Islamic countries and organisations condemned the attacks on the airport, warning that attacks threaten regional security and civil aviation safety and calling for international action to halt them and hold those responsible accountable. Qatar, Bahrain, Jordan and Lebanon, among others, strongly condemned the attacks. Besides, the Arab League, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation , the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Muslim World League also condemned the incident. In a statement today, Bangladesh's Foreign Minister said, "Attacks endangering civilian lives and targeting civilian infrastructure are unacceptable and must cease immediately." Bangladesh reiterated its firm solidarity with the government and the brotherly people of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the face of this attack. The Saudi-led coalition blamed Houthis for the attack, calling the strike a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response, reports AP. The fatalities also included one each from Palestine, the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. Today, Iran-backed Houthis urged airlines, travellers and airport workers to avoid Saudi airports. In a post on X, the Houthis warned that Saudi airports and airspace remained vulnerable to attacks, exempting airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. They also said Saudi Arabia would bear responsibility for any failed interceptions. The warning came amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. Saudi Arabia has increased its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. sources.evidenceText: The Farmers Services Centres initiative under the Feed Ghana Programme will be a game change for the nation’s agriculture, President John Dramani Mahama has said. He noted that when all the 50 Farmers Services Centres across the country become fully operational, Ghanaians would see a revolution in the nation’s agricultural practices. The President stated this in his remarks during an inspection tour of the Asunafo North Farmers Services Centre on day two of his two-day Resetting Ghana Tour of the Ahafo Region. He said under the initiative, mechanised agriculture equipment would be placed at each Farmers Services Centre to provide services to the farmers. The Government plans to roll out 50 Farmer Service Centres across agricultural districts nationwide, beginning with the first facility launched at Takoratwene in the Afram Plains in the Eastern Region. Mr Eric Opoku, the Minister of Food and Agriculture, said construction works were underway currently on 15 out of the 50 Farmers Services Centre, which would be operationalized by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

sources.evidenceText: The Chiefs and people of Ziope in the Agotime Ziope District of the Volta Region have undertaken an initiative aimed at building a technologically inclined community. The initiative saw the commissioning of a well-equipped self-help information and communication technology lab for the community basic school, aimed at providing all-round training for pupils. This would enable the pupils to study the practical aspects of ICT, unlike previously, when they only had the theory with illustrations on the boards. The Ziope Community, under the leadership of Dufia, Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV, instituted the Ngoryiza, 2024, to mobilise resources towards the development of the area. Noticing the significance of information and communication technology in today’s world, proceeds from the 2025 celebrations were directed at the construction of a lab. At the commissioning ceremony, Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV lauded the community’s enthusiasm towards initiatives aimed at enhancing the livelihoods of the residents. He identified their efforts towards the construction of a 4-unit nurses’ quarters to house staff posted to the community health centre, contributing to improved healthcare delivery in the area. He eulogised Rev Mensah Djokoto for providing forty desktop computers for the proposed ICT lab, which is furnished with an air conditioner, robotic logistics and an internet connection. “None of the public Junior High Schools in Ghana has this kind of logistics, as seen at the Ziope Basic School. I am happy we undertook this initiative to secure the future of our children and the Ziope community", he said. Togbe Kpoduave Ahiagba IV urged them to continue to contribute towards such development initiatives, to drive development in the Ziope community. “In unity we will find strength and development. If you bring a cedi and I bring a cedi, doesn't it become 2 cedis? Will your Cedi alone be able to do it? So we must continue on this agenda and not be tired as we have identified another project for next year”, he said. Rev Mensah Djokoto explained that he was touched and took the decision with a friend to make such a significant contribution to the education of pupils in the community, in an attempt to give back to society. He said that a zeal to ensure the pupils have an all-round ICT education prompted him to add coding and robotics to the centre, hence involving the Ghana Code Club. The Founder and Director of Ghana Code Club, Ernestina Edem Appiah, said a practical curriculum beginning with digital literacy and computational thinking, artificial intelligence, coding, robotics and electronics will be deployed, targeting how to train the pupils in creating with technology. “The children will learn to build programs and animations using tools such as Scratch; they will explore critical computing with tools such as micro: bit. They will learn the foundations of robotics, and gradually be introduced to AI, including how AI works, how it can be used responsibly, and how they can use emerging texts to create solutions to problems within their own communities”, she said. “We strongly believe that coding begins in their minds. So even before a child becomes confident with her computer, we tell them how to think logically and identify patterns. Break problems into smaller parts, experiment, make mistakes, and try again. That is a kind of learning we want the centre to be present”, she added. The Member of Parliament for Agotime Ziope, Charles Agvbeve, lauded the initiative, underscoring the need for communities to champion self-help projects, helping the government to develop the country. He expressed optimism about performance in the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) would improve as the “Agotime Ziope District scored first in 2025”, urging pupils of the final year students of the Ziope Basic School to score 1 in ICT in the 2026 BECE. He advised that the ICT lab should be used as a learning centre for pupils from other schools in the enclave to enhance their training as well. The Volta Regional Chairman of the National Democratic Congress, Mawutor Agbavitor, was elated with the initiative, acknowledging their efforts to lead the way in developing their community. He was enthused with their choice of enhancing ICT training of the pupils, as ”ICT is no longer a luxury but rather a necessity. The jobs of tomorrow, the knowledge of today, and the competition our children will face, all require digital skills.” The community launched the 2027 edition of the Ngoryiza, hoping to raise funds to tackle other social needs of the community.

sources.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. The clang of hammers and crowbars echoed across Alam-Khankandi village yesterday morning as families dismantled their own homes, racing against a river that has already devoured four char villages and is eating into a fifth. In two years, 1,803 families in five villages have lost their homes to erosion of char land beside the Padma Bridge. Of them, 303 families in Alam-Khankandi have been displaced since August, according to the Shariatpur Water Development Board (WDB) and Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. About 150 families still living in the village are at imminent risk. The char emerged about three decades ago in Painpara mouza on the northern bank of the Padma. According to WDB sources, the char formed Naodoba Union Parishad, which includes six villages and constitutes wards 2 and 3. During a visit yesterday, this correspondent found families preparing to leave. Those already homeless lived beside roads or in tin-sheet shelters on rented land, while others planned to cross the Padma by engine-run trawlers to rent land in Zajira or Munshiganj. Duluna Begum, 60, travelled from Digholi in Bikrampur, Munshiganj, after her daughter called her at night on her phone to tell her that her in-laws’ house was being devoured by the river. “I came here early in the morning with other people to help them dismantle the house before the river swallowed it whole,” she told The Daily Star. “Five days ago, nine bighas of cultivated land were lost in river erosion. Now where will my daughter go with her four children?” Maksuda Begum, 55, of Farazi Kandi in Zajira also came with helpers to dismantle her daughter’s in-laws’ house. For Md Shahid Fakir, 38, erosion destroyed both his livelihood and his house. He once owned 25 bighas, where he grew ginger, garlic, and vegetables, and a trawler to carry the produce across the river. “Having lost everything to river erosion, I am now destitute. I have no place to call my own anymore,” he said. He is now building a shack on land lent to him by someone. “If the government gave a little space to live on khas (government) land, then I could somehow spend my life raising a house there,” he said. Last year, erosion destroyed four villages in ward 2 of the union. They are Ahammad Majhikandi, Mongol Majhikandi, Alim Uddin Beparikandi, and Majhikandi, leaving around 1,500 families homeless. Painpara Government Primary School No 52 was washed away in August 2024, and about a year later Rezia Amin Government Primary School and a community clinic followed, said Altaf Hossain Khan, chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad. At least 5,000 acres of cropland in Painpara mouza have been lost over the past year, and No 122 Altaf Khan Government Primary School is now under threat, he added. A 4.5-kilometre paved road built in 2021 has lost four kilometres to the river. Electricity reached 1,200 consumers across the six villages through a 30-kilometre transmission line, including submarine cables along the riverbed, at a cost of Tk 4.5 crore. Nazmul Hasan, deputy general manager (technical) of Shariatpur Palli Bidyut Samity, said 22 kilometres of the line had been dismantled as villages disappeared. Another 3.5 kilometres were removed from the Alam-Khankandi area in the past three months to keep the line from falling into the river, though supply continued. Residents now living in the open without power can apply for reconnection under existing rules if they relocate near electricity poles, he said. The chairman of Purba Naodoba Union Parishad said residents had informed the WDB repeatedly about the erosion for the last 3-4 years, but saw no effective action from their part. He said some displaced families had moved to Louhajang in Munshiganj, while others rented homes or leased land in Shariatpur. At least 250 families who cannot afford either have taken shelter at a construction yard near the Padma Bridge’s southern end, living in fear as the Bangladesh Bridge Authority occasionally serves eviction notices. Appeals to the UNO and DC have yielded little, he said. With few jobs remaining nearby, many families struggle to eat adequately, he added. “The way the WDB treats us makes us feel like as though we are criminals. They do not answer our calls, nor do they want to speak to us even when they visit,” he said. MP Sayeed Ahmed distributed rice, lentils and dry food among 273 affected families about a month ago, the chairman said. WDB Executive Engineer Md Milton Hossain said the board was aware of the erosion and had informed higher authorities. “Protecting the mainland is our priority in cases of river erosion. That is why it is often not possible to take measures in char areas,” he said, adding that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures there. He said he would inspect the area and take necessary steps, subject to approval from higher authorities. ready.headline: ‘A living hell’: how Los Angeles got taken over by mosquitoes | Los Angeles

image.alt: ‘A living hell’: how Los Angeles got taken over by mosquitoes | Los Angeles

sources.title: ‘A living hell’: how Los Angeles got taken over by mosquitoes
sources.evidenceText: Heat and humidity have led to one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, with West Nile virus at a decade high Heat and humidity have led to one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, with West Nile virus at a decade high Los Angeles might be best known for blue skies, beaches and film premiers — but for the last several years it’s held another, unenviable distinction: the most mosquito-infested city in America . And this year has been especially nightmarish, thanks to a series of heatwaves and an extra-powerful El Niño . Locals have called it a summer of “ living hell ” as clouds of mosquitoes swarm backyards and leave diners at open air patios scratching their ankles. That double whammy of heat and humidity is making 2026 one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, causing a spike in cases of West Nile virus and raising fears that the nuisance bugs could spread other diseases including dengue , brought in by travelers. With moisture in this week’s forecast and overnight temperatures likely to stay above 50F (10C), there seems to be no end in sight for a problem that local authorities have struggled to contain for the last decade. “I’ve been here my whole life and the amount of mosquitoes I’ve seen this summer has been insane,” said one TikTok user in a video with more than 20,000 likes. “Everyone is talking about them … You can’t even go to your back yard. You can’t even sit in your car with the windows down. They’re infested everywhere.” Southern California residents have struggled all year to keep the winged bloodsuckers at bay. Some have resorted to sleeping in long sleeves after failing to kill off the mosquitoes that colonize their homes. Others have tried to seal off the cracks below their doors with towels . “It’s an absolute nightmare,” Truman Hedding, an El Segundo resident, told Fox 11 News earlier this year. “We invest a lot of money to live in a beautiful town like El Segundo. The last thing we want is to stay up all night fighting mosquitoes.” Los Angeles county has documented more than 180 cases of West Nile virus this year, according to the county public health department – the highest number in nearly a decade. And mosquito season is still far from over. “This year in particular for our area has been higher mosquito activity and higher disease activity,” said Anais Medina Diaz, communications director for the San Gabriel mosquito and vector control district. “We can attribute that to some connection to the environment and how warm it’s been this year – particularly because we had a very warm winter. Mosquito activity plummets when temperatures approach 50F overnight. But this winter was exceptionally mild, with heatwaves in February and March that allowed mosquitoes to stay active. The unusually moist and humid summer made it easier for them to reproduce. The region has sweltered under a record-breaking heatwave since early October, although forecasts show relief on the way. But the temperatures won’t drop low enough in most places to halt mosquito activity entirely, while coming rains will give them new places to breed. Southern California hasn’t always been such a mosquito hotspot. sources.evidenceText: Emergency Lawyers blames Egypt for the deadly attack in northern Sudan. An air raid at a gold mine near the disputed Sudan-Egypt border has killed at least 72 workers, according to a Sudanese rights group, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region. Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan’s war, accused the Egyptian military of carrying out the attack. “Egyptian fighter jets targeted civilian miners in the northern Wadi area inside Sudanese territory, resulting, according to preliminary information, in the killing of 72 civilians,” the Khartoum-based rights organisation wrote on X on Sunday. The reported attack on Saturday cannot be independently verified, and Egypt has issued no official comment. It was this year’s second attack on the mountainous border region of Jabal al-Uqaydat, a gold mining area. Similar strikes, also reportedly carried out by Egypt, killed 23 workers at the gold mining site in June. The Egyptian military said at the time that it had conducted a “large-scale operation” against illegal gold mining within its borders. The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halaib Triangle. Images shared on social media and by local rights groups, which could not be verified, showed dozens of bodies strewn in rubble and others wrapped in funeral shrouds. Miners described an air strike on the area. Since April 2023, the war in Sudan between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and created a humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides’ war efforts. The rugged mountainous area, home to bountiful mineral deposits, stretches for hundreds of kilometres and includes the disputed Halaib Triangle. Emergency Lawyers said the attack occurred within Sudanese territory. “The repeated attacks on the gold and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan’s natural resources,” it said. The Egyptian army said in June that it carried out its operation “within Egyptian territory”. It said 223 people were detained, including 136 foreign nationals, and announced a campaign to counter “illegal gold mining and arms smuggling” in the area. Despite backing Sudan’s army chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border – which stretches 1,200km (745 miles) from the Red Sea to Libya – a significant threat to its security. East of the Nile River, the porous border has for years been a thriving conduit for gold, illicit trade and human trafficking, which Egypt has tried to stem, including by using mass deportations.

The paramilitary group, which has been repeatedly accused of war crimes, ethnic cleansing and atrocities against civilians, has received military support from the United Arab Emirates, according to investigations by international human rights organisations. Abu Dhabi denies backing the RSF. UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan Denise Brown condemned the killings and demanded accountability for attacks on civilians. “Condemning these senseless killings is essential, but there must also be accountability for this flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law,” she said. “As each day goes by in this war, the world continues to accept the suffering of the people of Sudan.” The UN warned that the Abu Shandi area had already endured sustained attacks in recent weeks, forcing thousands of civilians to abandon their homes and leaving vulnerable communities exposed to further violence. The RSF-led alliance has denied responsibility for the latest strike. The latest killings have renewed attention on the RSF’s relationship with the UAE, whose alleged military support for the paramilitary group has become one of the most contentious aspects of Sudan’s civil war. Investigations by Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and international media organisations have documented evidence of weapons supplies, logistical assistance and foreign fighters linked to the UAE reaching RSF forces. Sudan’s internationally recognised government has repeatedly accused Abu Dhabi of fuelling the conflict by supplying the RSF with weapons and military assistance, allegations the UAE continues to reject. Emirati authorities maintain that they are not supporting either side militarily and insist their involvement in Sudan is focused on humanitarian assistance and diplomatic efforts to end the fighting. Sudan descended into civil war in April 2023 following a power struggle between army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. The Sudanese army has since regained control of much of the country’s central and eastern regions, while the RSF retains significant territory in the western Darfur region and parts of southern Sudan. Around 825,000 children are also at risk of severe acute malnutrition as fighting, insecurity and restrictions on humanitarian access continue to deepen the emergency. Repeated attacks have forced thousands of residents to flee towards displacement sites, where overcrowding, food shortages and inadequate medical facilities have left families increasingly vulnerable. sources.evidenceText: Thirty people were killed and at least 18 were injured by Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine that included an attack on a public bus, authorities said Thursday, as an intensive pre-winter wave of attacks continued and power outages worsened in the capital Kyiv. Ukrainian authorities set up netting to stop the drone attacks, according to the Associated Press Ukraine news director. Vadym Filashkin, head of the regional military administration, said public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighboring city of Sloviansk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, was halted because of the sharp deterioration in security. He accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, adding: “In such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers. The safety of residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is above all.” The attacks follow deadly missile strikes a day earlier in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky, where the death toll rose to 22, including five children. Rescuers searched through the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missile and at least 54 people were injured. Heavy debris was removed from the cratered section of the building, while rescue dogs continued a search nearby for residents who have not yet been accounted for. Several survivors of the attack were forced to sleep in heavily damaged apartments after they couldn't find anywhere else to sleep. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries. “It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine’s defense,” he wrote in an online post. “Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day.” Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Separately, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.

sources.evidenceText: A large-scale Russian missile and drone assault struck Ukraine's capital and the surrounding Kyiv Oblast overnight, killing at least 17 people and injuring 44 others, authorities confirmed on Wednesday. The overnight attack, one of the most intense in recent weeks, involved a barrage of ballistic missiles, hypersonic missiles, and attack drones that targeted Kyiv and nearby districts, causing widespread destruction and prompting ongoing search-and-rescue operations. According to Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS), at least 14 people were killed and 27 others injured in Kyiv Oblast, where emergency crews continued to search damaged buildings for survivors. In the capital, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko initially reported one death and 24 injuries. Later, President Volodymyr Zelensky updated the nationwide casualty toll, saying that at least 17 people had been killed and 44 injured in the attack, though he did not provide a district-by-district breakdown. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 24 ballistic missiles, four hypersonic missiles, and 115 Shahed-type attack drones during the overnight assault. The military said none of the ballistic missiles were intercepted, underscoring the growing strain on Ukraine's air defense capabilities. "The main target of the attack was the warehouses of civilian enterprises. There were also strikes on infrastructure and a railway station," Zelensky said in a statement posted on social media. The Ukrainian president renewed calls for additional Western air defense support, arguing that the shortage of interceptor missiles has left the country increasingly vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile attacks. "Ballistic interceptors are something that could have saved the lives of those who died today. It is very important that partners realize that delays in their delivery or unwillingness to transfer anti-ballistics leads to such terrible victims and destruction," Zelensky said. Ukraine has repeatedly warned that it faces a critical shortage of interceptor missiles for its Patriot air defense systems—the only systems currently capable of intercepting ballistic missiles. Ukrainian officials say Russia has intensified its use of ballistic weapons in recent weeks, seeking to exploit those shortages. Authorities reported extensive destruction across Kyiv and surrounding areas. The State Emergency Service said warehouses, commercial facilities, and vehicles were set ablaze in the Brovary, Bucha, and Fastiv districts of Kyiv Oblast. Within the capital, damage was recorded at more than seven locations, including the Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Desnianskyi, and Sviatoshynskyi districts, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. In the Holosiivskyi district, rescue teams pulled two people from beneath the rubble of a collapsed warehouse, while search operations continued amid concerns that additional victims remained trapped. A missile strike ignited a fire in a 20-story residential building in the Obolonskyi district, where another apartment building and two warehouse facilities also caught fire. In the Desnianskyi district, a warehouse was engulfed in flames, while missile debris landed near a residential building, Mayor Klitschko said. Emergency responders also battled a major fire in the Kyiv-Sviatoshynskyi district outside the capital. Among those injured in Kyiv, 15 people were hospitalized, including four in critical condition, city officials said. Residents reported hearing the first powerful explosions shortly after 12:20 a.m. local time as multiple ballistic missiles struck Kyiv. Explosions continued for more than an hour while Ukraine's Air Force repeatedly warned that additional ballistic missiles were approaching the capital. Beginning at 1:09 a.m. local time, authorities also issued alerts for incoming Shahed attack drones as the assault expanded. The latest bombardment came just days after another large-scale Russian missile strike on Kyiv on Aug. 1 that killed at least nine people and injured more than 30 others, highlighting the continued escalation of Russia's long-range attacks on the Ukrainian capital despite ongoing international efforts to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses. sources.title: Rooppur Unit-1 achieves first nuclear chain reaction
sources.evidenceText: The first controlled nuclear chain reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was achieved today (11 October), marking a major milestone in Bangladesh's first nuclear power project as the reactor entered its initial criticality stage ahead of electricity generation. The chain reaction marks the first of four stages before the plant can generate electricity. The subsequent stages involve thermal energy transfer, mechanical energy conversion, and finally electricity generation and supply to the national grid. Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, confirmed the development to The Business Standard, saying the reaction was initiated after the required compliance procedures, technical parameters and external certifications had been completed. "Today at 3:34pm, we were able to achieve the chain reaction smoothly. By the grace of Allah, the parameters were within the desired ranges, and the reactor was very stable," he said. Inside a nuclear reactor, a controlled chain reaction splits uranium atoms through nuclear fission, releasing energy as heat. That heat is used to generate steam, which drives turbines to produce electricity. Russian specialists, Bangladeshi experts and other technical specialists were present to observe the process and assess the reactor's performance, Anwar added. He said nuclear fuel had already been loaded into the reactor and the fission process had now begun. Anwar said technical teams were working to complete the remaining processes as quickly as possible, while stressing that every stage must comply with the required procedures and safety standards. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Ishwardi, Pabna, is being built with two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units using Russian technology supplied by Rosatom. sources.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy Bangladesh's first nuclear power plant, located at Rooppur in Pabna's Ishwardi, has made significant progress toward initiating nuclear fission in its first unit after regulators approved the results of safety valve tests, paving the way for the next phase of commissioning. If work proceeds according to the plan, the plant could begin supplying electricity to the national grid on a trial basis as early as next month, project officials said. The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200 megawatts (MW). Once both units are fully operational, they are expected to contribute a combined 2,400 MW to the national grid, diversify the country's energy mix and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Officials concerned with the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) said the initiation of heat production through nuclear fission in the first unit had initially been planned for September. However, technical defects identified during safety valve testing delayed the next stage of work. Following two rounds of high-pressure testing, the results were submitted to the regulatory authority, which approved them last Thursday, the project officials said. The tests assessed whether the control valves were functioning according to prescribed standards. Fire safety and radiation protection arrangements were also examined as part of the process. The approval allows the project to proceed with further reactor commissioning activities. However, the officials said that achieving first criticality, gradually increasing reactor power, starting the turbine and supplying electricity to the national grid are separate stages, each requiring the completion of relevant technical and safety checks. The next major milestone is 'first criticality', when a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction is established inside the reactor. A series of tests and observations will follow - a process that could take around a month. Reactor power will then be increased gradually. Initially, the plant is expected to supply around 300 MW to the national grid on a trial basis. Further testing and technical assessments will be required before the facility reaches commercial operation. Built with technical assistance from Russia, Rooppur uses third-generation VVER-1200 reactor technology. Project estimates suggest that the plant could meet around 10 percent of Bangladesh's electricity demand when both units are operational at full capacity. Its actual contribution will depend on national demand, plant performance, maintenance schedules and grid conditions. Unlike coal-, oil- or gas-fired power plants, nuclear facilities generate heat through the fission of uranium atoms rather than by burning fossil fuels. The heat produces steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electricity-generating system. Rooppur is designed for an operational life of 60 years, potentially extendable by another 20 to 30 years, subject to technical upgrades, safety assessments and regulatory approval. Routine maintenance and fuel replacement will remain essential, with refuelling potentially required approximately every 18 months. Sheikh Mohammad Touhidul Islam, joint secretary (Nuclear Power Wing) of the Ministry of Science and Technology, told BSS that Rooppur was not merely an electricity generation project but also a major opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's technological capabilities and develop skilled human resources. He said the first unit was in the final stages of preparation for generation, while uranium for the second unit had also arrived at the project site. He expressed hope that work could be completed ahead of schedule. Additional Secretary of the ministry Abul Khair Md Akkas Ali said the plant could reshape Bangladesh's electricity and economic landscape, supporting industrial production, attracting investment and creating employment opportunities. Science and Technology Secretary Md Anwar Hossain described Rooppur as a historic milestone for the country's energy security and economic progress, highlighting its potential to support reliable electricity supplies and peaceful applications of nuclear technology. The project has a long history, with feasibility studies and international cooperation initiatives dating back to the years following the independence. The arrival of nuclear fuel at the site in October 2023 marked a major step towards commissioning. The BNP's 2008 election manifesto also included a pledge to establish the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant. Similarly, the party's 2026 election manifesto advocates for the continued peaceful use of nuclear energy in the power and energy sectors. As the first unit approaches its initial operational milestone, Rooppur is expected to play an increasingly important role in Bangladesh's long-term energy strategy, provided that all commissioning stages are completed in accordance with safety requirements and regulatory standards. The Ministry of Science and Technology's Nuclear Power Wing oversees and coordinates project progress on behalf of the government, while Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom provides technical assistance.

sources.title: Fresh Nepal flash flood washes away houses and bridges with five missing
sources.evidenceText: Some locals told The Kathmandu Post they had alerted one another to the flood nearly an hour before official notifications came in. Suna Gurung was awakened at 04:45 on Sunday by a call from someone in a riverside village upstream, saying a river had burst its banks and urging him to flee immediately. "Within ten minutes, the river swelled dramatically in the dark. We raised an alarm, woke everyone up, and fled into the forest," Gurung told The Kathmandu Post. "By the time I received the government SMS on my phone warning us to stay safe, we had already been sheltering in the forest for over an hour." Nepali authorities acknowledged the delay in alerting the public. Alerts were sent to residents in higher regions nearly two hours after the floods began, while messages to lower regions were dispatched nearly five hours later, they say. This, as with previous disasters, highlights the deficiencies Nepal's early-warning system faces, often forcing residents in rural communities to rely on informal networks and social media.

sources.title: Nepal orders evacuations after landslide triggers Budhi Gandaki flash flood | Africanews
sources.evidenceText: Nepal’s authorities ordered evacuations along the Budhi Gandaki River on Sunday, 11 October, after sudden flooding swept away homes and other buildings in the country’s mountainous north-central region. Villagers fled to higher ground as the swollen river surged through narrow valleys. Aerial footage released by the Nepal Army showed floodwaters racing between mountains and residents being evacuated to safety. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority warned communities to remain alert until late Sunday. No deaths were immediately reported, although several people were listed as missing. Preliminary accounts suggested the flooding was triggered when a landslide blocked the river near Chumchure, in Gorkha district, before the temporary barrier gave way. The latest emergency comes as Nepal struggles to recover from devastating floods along its border with China in August, which killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Nearly 33,000 people were affected, with around 7,500 homes damaged or destroyed. The government estimates reconstruction will cost $4.77 billion. Authorities are now focusing on restoring roads and bridges damaged in the earlier disaster, particularly in remote areas where disrupted transport links have made delivering aid difficult.

Mongabay traveled to Chile’s Patagonia National Park to follow a women-led team on a mission to bring 13 Darwin’s rheas back to the wild in April 2026. Working with Rewilding Chile Foundation , these dedicated rangers care for the birds around the clock, facing harsh weather, predators like pumas, illegal livestock grazing, and other threats to the park’s fragile ecosystem. For more than a century, the Chacabuco Valley, where the park is located, was dominated by sheep and cattle ranching. Fences fragmented the vast Patagonian steppes and rheas (Rhea pennata) nearly disappeared. But one of South America’s most ambitious rewilding efforts is helping to turn the tide. Tompkins Conservation, the organization behind Rewilding Chile, acquired former ranchlands and began removing thousands of kilometers of fencing, allowing native wildlife to reclaim the landscape. Now, the team is preparing for another milestone: Releasing 13 Darwin’s rheas into the wild. Mongabay followed the rangers in the days leading up to the release, documenting their preparations, the challenges they faced, and their determination to give these birds the best possible chance of survival. ready.headline: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk

sources.title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
sources.evidenceText: edited by Sadie Harley , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. The research was led by scientists from the University of Chicago, Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Bonn and Ohio University. Using high-resolution microCT imaging, the team reconstructed the skull and skeletal anatomy of the fossil. They discovered an unexpected combination of traits. Megacauda had specialized blade-like cheek teeth resembling those of modern seals, a platypus-like pelvis and an otter-like tail, indicating it was likely a semiaquatic predator that hunted small vertebrates and invertebrates in freshwater environments. More significantly, the researchers identified a pair of small bony projections on the roof of the mouth that closely resemble features found in living therian mammals, a group that includes marsupials (such as kangaroos and opossums) and placental mammals (such as elephants and humans). In modern mammals, these structures help support the soft palate and muscles involved in suckling, swallowing and protecting the airway. Because soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, scientists have long struggled to determine when these important feeding structures first evolved. "The anatomy of Megacauda suggests that structures involved in coordinating swallowing and sucking had already begun to evolve by the Middle Jurassic. This discovery helps us better understand the biological foundations of one of the defining characteristics of mammals: feeding young with milk," said Zhe-Xi Luo, Ph.D., professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study. The researchers also found highly specialized hyoid bones in the throat region. In living mammals, these bones help anchor muscles for swallowing. Together, the evidence suggests that Megacauda likely possessed an early version of the coordinated muscular system used by modern mammals to move milk and food safely from the mouth to the esophagus. The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about how these structures evolved. Researchers found that the newly identified therian-like bony hooks existed alongside more primitive bony ridges known from earlier mammaliaforms and mammalian ancestors. Their coexistence in the same animal suggests the modern structures did not evolve directly from the primitive ridges as previously believed. "This fossil captures an important stage in mammalian evolution," said Luo. "For decades, scientists have wanted to know when the soft-tissue structures necessary for suckling and complex swallowing first appeared. Megacauda provides some of the clearest evidence yet that many of these innovations emerged well before the rise of modern mammals." The research also has important implications for understanding living mammals. While therian mammals use a sophisticated suckling mechanism supported by the soft palate and constrictor muscles, monotremes such as platypuses and echidnas use a different method for obtaining milk and lack some of these anatomical features. The new evidence suggests that monotremes likely lost elements of the ancestral suckling apparatus during their evolutionary history and developed an alternative method of milk intake. Beyond feeding biology, Megacauda highlights the remarkable ecological diversity of mammaliaforms living alongside dinosaurs. At approximately the size of a modern otter, it is among the largest known Jurassic mammaliaforms and represents one of the earliest examples of adaptation to a semiaquatic lifestyle. "These discoveries continue to reveal that the age of dinosaurs was also a time of extraordinary evolutionary innovation among early mammals," said Peishu Li, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the Ohio University Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine and a co-author of the study. sources.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
sources.imageAlt: Exterior view of the International Criminal Court
sources.evidenceText: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". "[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals. While the physical damage from Houthi attacks can be quickly repaired, the Saudi reputation for stability is taking a battering. Ukraine's leader had said the deal with Russia to release diesel into the US would help Moscow fund the war. Roofs were ripped off buildings after Isaias barrelled into the US on Friday evening, before it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone. All but one of those who died, including the gunman, were related, police say. A motive for the shooting is not yet known. The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world".

sources.title: US sanctions International Criminal Court in major escalation
sources.imageAlt: US sanctions International Criminal Court in major escalation
sources.evidenceText: Latest action seeks to stem resources to international tribunal Trump administration has vowed to dismantle. Washington, DC – United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has announced a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), this time targeting the entity itself, as opposed to the tribunal’s officials or groups that provide support. The announcement on Friday represented a major escalation from the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has vowed an “all of government” approach to dismantling the court. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on social media. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” As justification for its actions, the administration has pointed to the court’s ongoing investigation into abuses committed in Afghanistan, which could ensnare US military and intelligence personnel, as well as the ICC’s arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes committed in Gaza. Before Friday’s actions, the US had sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court. Several rights groups have challenged those sanctions in US federal court, saying restricting how US citizens interact with the court treads on their constitutional freedoms. Sanctioned ICC judges have also launched legal challenges in the US. Speaking to the Reuters news agency on Friday, deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan said the sanctions “must be condemned”. “The sanctions are intended to undermine ⁠⁠⁠⁠the rule of ⁠⁠⁠⁠law internationally and the work that an ⁠⁠⁠⁠independent judicial institution ⁠⁠⁠⁠is doing,” ⁠⁠⁠⁠Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our ‌‌‌‌situations, our investigations and our ‌‌‌‌prosecutions.” In a statement, the ICC called on member states to redouble support. “History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack,” it said. The US and Israel are not parties to the Rome Statute, the founding treaty that establishes the court’s jurisdiction. However, the court has long ruled that abuses committed by US or Israeli citizens in the territories of countries that are ICC members can be prosecuted. Israel was among those cheering the Trump administration’s latest action. “Thank you for your leadership,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement posted on social media. To date, the court has not sought to prosecute any US citizens. A US law dating back to 2002, amid the so-called “Global War on Terror”, already prohibits extradition of US citizens to be tried by the ICC. It further authorises the use of military force in the event that a US citizen is held in detention while being prosecuted by the court, in what critics have dubbed the “Hague invasion clause”. Nevertheless, some US administrations, particularly those led by Democrats, have sought to provide support for the court and have espoused its founding principles. Rights observers have said that the US pressure campaign could have wide-ranging implications for the court’s investigations, particularly the network of local organisations and fact-finders upon which it relies to build cases. Mark Kersten, an international law expert and professor at the University of Fraser Valley in British Columbia, Canada, said ICC advocates have feared direct sanctions on the court itself since Trump took office for his second term in January last year. “This was the number one concern: the possibility not only that individuals would be sanctioned, but that the court itself would be sanctioned,” he told Al Jazeera. “That should give people a sense of the significance of this…the worst-case scenario has come about”. The US has also urged other countries to withdraw from the court, suggesting it would assess allies’ relationship with the court when determining foreign assistance. The appeal has dovetailed with wariness from some ICC members over what they have called the unequal application of international law, with offenders in the Global South more likely to face accountability. In July, Chad and Venezuela moved to withdraw from the court, following Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. The years ahead, Kersten said, will be a test of support from ICC members, who will need to intervene to circumvent the US sanctions. Most of Europe, Latin America and large areas of Africa remain members of the tribunal, as do Canada and Australia. “Only with the support and concrete action of those states will the court really ultimately survive,” he said. The latest round of sanctions means that companies that provide services to the court could be penalised. Sanctioning the entire entity, which has about 900 staff, as opposed to individual officials, will make it more difficult for the court to insulate itself from such sanctions. The sanctions block “all property and interests in property” the court has in the US, while prohibiting “making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit” of the court. The sanctions included several temporary exemptions, including for services providing maintenance, technology and pension plans. The State Department said the exemptions are meant to “provide time for States Parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC”. William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University in London, said it was not immediately clear how impactful the sanctions would be

sources.evidenceText: Member Countries Should Renew Support for Court, Minimize Harm Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC) is an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law, Human Rights Watch said today. On October 9, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the imposition of sanctions on the ICC. “The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court,” said Philippe Bolopion , executive director of Human Rights Watch. “By attacking the court, the US government is threatening justice for victims of abuses from Palestine to Ukraine, Myanmar, and Sudan.” The ICC is a permanent international court created to try people, including senior officials, accused of war crimes , crimes against humanity , genocide, and the crime of aggression. Following the genocides in the mid-1990s in Rwanda and in the former Yugoslavia, the international community created the ICC to prevent those most responsible for serious crimes from evading justice. Nearly two-thirds of UN member countries have joined the court. In addition to its Palestine investigation, the court has opened investigations into alleged crimes in 17 situations , including in Afghanistan , Darfur in Sudan , Bangladesh/Myanmar , Ukraine , and Venezuela . The US government’s decision to sanction the ICC was announced on the same day that the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Navi Pillay , a former ICC judge and renowned international lawyer, in recognition of her central role “in ensuring that war crimes , crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.” In his October 9 announcement, Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza. Palestine became an ICC member in 2015 and gave the court a mandate to address serious crimes committed on its territory or by its nationals since June 13, 2014. The Trump administration has already sanctioned ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges, three prominent Palestinian human rights groups, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and called on ICC member countries to leave the court. US sanctions have serious effects on those targeted, including frozen or closed bank accounts, rejected financial transactions, denied access to digital services, and US entry bans. US sanctions also have a chilling effect on non-US banks and other companies outside of US jurisdiction that could themselves lose access to the US banking system if they do not adhere to the sanctions. This means that the ICC could lose access to companies on which it relies for everyday functions, from banking to information, technology to travel. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed a lawsuit in US federal court on August 11, 2026, seeking to have the sanctions regime previously used to authorize court-wide sanctions struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit. ICC member countries , including the Netherlands which hosts the ICC in The Hague, the leadership body of the court’s Assembly of States Parties , the European Union , UN human rights experts , the UN secretary-general , the UN high commissioner for human rights , civil society organizations , and the ICC itself have repeatedly spoken out against the sanctions. The ICC and its member countries have also taken important steps to insulate the court from the potential impact of sanctions, but more action is needed to protect the court’s ability to continue its critical work. The EU should immediately activate its blocking statute , which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions. The Trump administration’s sanctions targeting international justice are part of a broader attack on the laws, institutions, and organizations created to protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said. The United States has also withdrawn from the Paris Climate Accords and the World Health Organization , while disengaging from the UN Human Rights Council . President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have also expressed contempt for international law , and threatened to commit war crimes . “The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, can escape justice for the worst crimes,” Bolopion said. “Governments everywhere should take every available measure to counter the effects of the US sanctions and stand with the court and those relying on it to obtain justice.” UK and US Forced Displacement of the Chagossians and Ongoing Colonial Crimes Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer Human Rights Watch defends the rights of people in close to 100 countries worldwide, spotlighting abuses and bringing perpetrators to justice Get updates on human rights issues from around the globe. sources.evidenceText: United States President Donald Trump has made a surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine he says is "effective immediately", but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy says he is still waiting to see details of the deal. There was no word from Moscow on the ceasefire announcement on Sunday, which followed days of intense pressure from Trump for Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries. He blames those strikes for a rise in diesel prices that is hurting his Republican Party ahead of US midterm elections next month. In a dramatic deterioration in relations, Trump on Saturday warned Zelenskiy that he had "better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, and urged Ukrainians to replace their leader at new elections. Trump said Zelenskiy had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but did not elaborate further. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote. RISING GLOBAL FUEL PRICES Trump, whose war in Iran which began at the end of February has been widely blamed for hiking global fuel prices, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September, although neither side ever confirmed that such an agreement had been reached. A person familiar with the situation said the US had threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine as well as weapons procurement under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) system, as it pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian energy sites. The US threats were earlier reported by the Financial Times. The person added that Zelenskiy was speaking to European leaders about de-escalating the situation with Trump. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Zelenskiy said he had discussed Trump's ceasefire announcement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side," he said on Telegram. Speaking in his nightly video address, Zelenskiy said Russian forces were still launching air attacks on energy infrastructure, including a strike on a joint heating and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. A Ukrainian official confirmed the attack had taken place after Trump's announcement of the ceasefire. Hours earlier, Zelenskiy had pushed back against US pressure for a unilateral end to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, repeating his long-standing position that he was willing to do so only if President Vladimir Putin suspended Russian strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure. PROMISE OF ELECTIONS Trump also called for elections in Ukraine, suspended since the 2022 Russian invasion, to which Zelenskiy responded that he would call a vote if Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. Zelenskiy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader, but added that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskiy said. The Ukrainian leader rejected that he was to blame for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor. The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress. On Saturday, Zelenskiy responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and cost more lives. Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. Several US lawmakers also criticised the diesel deal. US Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, said the diesel supply deal with Russia may be illegal and will put American lives at risk. On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. "No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks. Ukrainian officials reported new Russian attacks on Sunday, killing three people outside a grocery store in Kharkiv and three in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk. Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, reported a new incursion by what officials said were Russian drones, landing only about 35km from the capital Chisinau.
