sources.evidenceText: NEW DELHI: Leaders of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country’s election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi. The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilization following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party. The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing. Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city. Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports. “We will not back down,” Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release. “We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests,” he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns. Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed. Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions “unacceptable.” “Covering events of public interest is not a crime,” RSF said in a statement. “It is their job.” In July, protests organized by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. Ahead of Saturday’s rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored. “I was detained for 10 hours yesterday,” said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. “I have come again today because it is important to show up.” The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain “peace for one year,” Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post. The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday’s detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally. “Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure,” Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks. The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to Internet connectivity as seen on Saturday. The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party. Soon after his release, the CJP’s Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him “an embarrassment to India.” “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said in a social media post. The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi — a comment the Indian government called “misplaced.” Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with “every single person who believes in democracy.” “There is nothing to fear,” he said on social media. “These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us.” Stay on top of the issues that matter to you the most.

In Mozambique , freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014 , a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique . However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience. In music, for example, this contradiction is clear. Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo . More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s , but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party. Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces. Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?” This is not just a provocative artistic comment. It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences. Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically. While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum , digital platforms for monitoring local governance , cultural associations, and artistic initiatives. This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces. However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order. One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools . The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered. By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity. During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest. In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions. However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent. In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity. When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk. This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.” Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost. Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival. In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value. It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity. The Mozambican Constitution affirms the right of all citizens to freedom of expression and opinion. But a democracy is not measured only by rights on paper, but also by the real conditions in which they can be exercised. Seventeen years ago, a char emerged in Purba Naodoba union of Zajira upazila in Shariatpur. On it grew a village called Alam Kha Kandi, and in 2017, the No 122 Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School was built there on 33 decimals of land. Back then, the Padma river was nearly two kilometres away -- not visible from the school gate. That distance has been vanishing. Over the past two years, successive bouts of erosion have dragged the river steadily closer, and it now licks at the school's own grounds, just 50 metres from the building. Teachers, students and local residents fear what has already happened twice nearby -- in 2024 and 2025, two primary schools in neighbouring villages of the same union were lost to the river. Painpara Government Primary School in union was swallowed by the river in August 2024; exactly a year later, in August 2025, Rizia Amin Government Primary School, also in Painpara, met the same fate. On a recent visit, the national flag still stood tall outside the erosion-battered school on the Padma's bank. But the earthen edge of the school field was crumbling into the water, and several trees lay broken along the bank. Nearby, the collapsed roof of a building the river had already claimed leaned forlornly against the shore. Inside, the signs of panic were unmistakable. The tin fencing had been dismantled to allow for a quick relocation if needed. The partition between two classrooms had been removed, and the overhead fans taken down. In the open space that remained, two teachers taught two separate classes side by side, children seated on either side of the room. At that moment, young voices could be heard reciting after their teacher: "Our little river flows in bends and turns, in the month of Boishakh it has knee-deep water." The children studied with evident joy -- but the irony of the verse was not lost on the adults around them. Erosion anxiety follows the students constantly, teachers said, and with the school itself at risk, safety concerns run alongside the lessons. Staff must now watch the river even as they teach. "The river keeps eroding and has come right onto our school field," said Borna Akter, a fourth-grade student, speaking to The Daily Star. "Our school could break apart at any time. It feels very scary, wondering when our school will break down. If our school goes into the river, we won't be able to study here anymore. Where will we study then? We want arrangements made to protect our school." School teacher Naimur Rahman Khan said panic over the erosion alone had already driven at least 100 students away. "We also always have to remain anxious, because the school is at risk," he said. "Even after we go home at the end of the day, we have to phone local residents to check on the river situation because arrangements for relocating the school must be made before it is lost to the river. If the school could be protected now, even by dropping some sandbags, children could attend classes here without fear." Altaf Hossain Khan, the school's founder and chairman of the union parishad, said the area had been eroding for years. "The river has now come close to the school. We have repeatedly requested the Water Development Board, but they have taken no action," he told The Daily Star over the phone. "If nothing is done now, the school could break apart and go into the riverbed at any moment." Md Milton Hossain, executive engineer of the Shariatpur Water Development Board, said the erosion in Alam Kha Kandi had been reported to higher authorities, but that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures in char areas. He added that no No Objection Certificate had been sought from the BWDB before the school was built on the char, and that neither the district nor the upazila education departments had alerted his office that the school was at risk. "Even so, I will visit the area and take the necessary measures, subject to permission from higher authorities," he said. Zajira Upazila Primary Education Officer Bazlur Rahman confirmed the school was at risk. "We have made preparations to relocate the school before erosion occurs, and another site is being sought," he told The Daily Star. "I will also request the concerned department to attempt to protect the school from the erosion." sources.evidenceText: What if the syllabics of the Cree language dominated everyday communication? This is the question asked by Joi T. Arcand’s new exhibition at the Carleton University Art Gallery. A key feature of the exhibition, which will run until Dec. 13, is a mural portraying a convenience store with signs rendered in Cree syllabics. Arcand says she was inspired by the Cree language's lack of visibility in Canadian society. "English or French is expected of us. We should have the same kind of access and representation of our own languages," she told CBC. "I got the idea to create this sort of utopic future, or alternate present, where our languages are in a healthy state." Arcand is an internationally renowned artist from Muskeg Lake First Nation in Saskatchewan. Her work has been exhibited across Canada and in Australia, South Korea and the United States. She's the former director of SAW Gallery’s Nordic Lab in Ottawa and has also worked on curatorial projects in Sweden. Arcand has been working on the current exhibition for four years alongside the Carleton art gallery’s acting director, Heather Anderson. The gallery is nearing its 35th anniversary and holds more than 30, 000 pieces of art in its collection. Anderson told CBC that Arcand’s work with Cree syllabics emerged from a 2009 photography called Here on Future Earth, where Arcand used photo-editing software to project signs with the language of Plains Cree onto buildings in Saskatchewan. Increasing visibility of Indigenous language is evident elsewhere on Carleton’s campus, including the renaming of the University Centre to Nideyinàn and Robertson Hall to Pigiarvik (ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᒃ). sources.evidenceText: Submerged trees in the catchment area of the Ken River near the Majhgawan Dam in Ajaygarh, Madhya Pradesh state, on Sept 20. AJAYGARH, India – Standing knee-deep in the Ken River, with mud smeared on her face to symbolise a connection to land her family has farmed for more than a century, Bitti Bai Kondar is among hundreds of tribal residents voicing anger over an US$87 billion (S$111 billion) government project to link India’s rivers. The mother of four adult sons, who are all protesting with her, has watched as rising water from work on the project has flooded her village. But the protesters say they would rather die than leave their ancestral home without better compensation. “The government is taking our land and water without giving us another place to live,” said Kondar, who is among scores of women who have shown their defiance by lying on mock funeral pyres. “They’re digging up our soil to build their dam, but they’re not giving us enough compensation to rebuild our lives.” The dispute is an early test for India’s ambitious plan to link some 30 rivers nationwide, which has been decades in the making but gathered momentum only in recent years, championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The aim is to redistribute water to drought-prone regions, boosting food security by aiding tens of millions of farmers in a country where agriculture remains a major employer. Critics say the programme risks uprooting communities and damaging fragile ecosystems. Connecting Madhya Pradesh state’s Ken River to Uttar Pradesh state’s Betwa River is phase one, with a cost of about US$4.6 billion. The government has offered residents along the Ken River in Panna district, Madhya Pradesh, at least 1.25 million Indian rupees (S$16,500) a hectare, more than double the initial offer of 500,000 rupees. Usha Parmar, the district administrator, said compensation to over 90% of people had already been paid. However, some residents argue that the payments do not cover all their losses. Dhaniram Bhatnagar, a local priest, said the temple where he worked had been completely submerged. “The temple was my only source of income and now it is gone,” he said. “The compensation offered by the government is only for my home, and that is not enough.” Environmentalists have long opposed the project, saying the proposed 2km-long Daudhan Dam on the Ken River will inundate some 9,000ha of land, including a significant portion of the Panna Tiger Reserve, one of India’s most successful tiger conservation programmes. The government has said the environmental impact is “unavoidable”, but can be mitigated through tree planting, wildlife conservation and other measures. Some critics even question the scientific basis for the multibillion-dollar plan. “There is a big question mark over this project’s feasibility because it rests on a hydrological presumption: a surplus in the Ken basin and a deficit in the Betwa basin,” said Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People. “That presumption has never been conclusively established.” A government spokeswoman said she could not immediately comment on the scientific assumptions underpinning the project and referred Reuters to an Aug 21 statement that said the project would help address chronic water scarcity in the Bundelkhand region, providing irrigation, drinking water and hydropower. sources.evidenceText: The world is flooded with debt, but while the U.S. and Europe have caused angst on global markets lately, China’s fiscal situation isn’t looking so great either. In fact, China’s debt has shot up so much in recent years that interest payments on all its borrowing are commanding a bigger share of public spending. Debt-servicing payments will account for 19.2% of the central government’s general public budget this year, up from 12% in 2014, according to new Conference Board estimates cited by the Financial Times . That tracks with a separate report earlier this year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies , which also found that 19% of Beijing’s spending is earmarked for interest on debt. That’s more than the 14% of the U.S. federal budget that goes to interest costs, though less than Japan’s 25.6%. CSIS added that China’s spending on interest payments skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025, faster than any other major budget category. By comparison, total spending jumped 102% in that span, with outlays on social security and employment up 207%, science and technology up 137%, and defense up 141%. To be sure, U.S. debt-interest spending looks grim too and has surged about 390% since 2013 to $1 trillion, which also tops the Pentagon’s budget. But the world’s two biggest economies have been diverging in key ways with implications for future growth and indebtedness. The U.S. economy is accelerating, helped by the AI boom, and despite high inflation, resilient consumers have continued to spend. Unemployment is low and signals full employment, while stock markets are at or near record highs. Of course, hyperscalers are racing to issue bonds to fund their data centers and chip purchases, but they are also raising money with fresh stock offerings and IPOs. Meanwhile, China’s GDP has been decelerating and is on pace to undercut its annual target of 4.5%-5%. And while export-facing sectors are growing at a fast clip, trade partners are putting up barriers, Chinese consumers remain reluctant to spend, investment is weak, the property sector is still digging out from an epic crash, and Chinese stocks have been anemic. Beijing has also steered state banks to provide financing to priority industries like electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence and renewable energy. sources.evidenceText: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. sources.evidenceText: Lorne Scott calls his farm an island. Given that it’s in the prairie pothole region of southern Saskatchewan – a sweep of shallow wetlands left by glaciers – this is a metaphor, but it works: in all directions from where we stand, on a sunny day in June, are cultivated croplands. They’ve been planted to within an inch of their lives with canola, wheat, lentils. Except for a few shelterbelts, there are no trees from here to the horizon. Then there’s Scott’s land, thick with trees, shrubs and grasses. Parts of his farm grow wild, or “never broke,” as he puts it, with aspen, snowberry, starflower, Solomon’s seal and northern bedstraw, from which the Cree, who were here before settlement, made red dye. The bedstraw seeds, when roasted, work as a coffee substitute. Scott doesn’t drink coffee. Nor does he harvest any of the Indigenous plants on his land, which sits about nine kilometres south of Indian Head and about 75 kilometres southeast of Regina. They’re just here, left to grow any which way. His land is wild on purpose. It’s fair to call Scott a conservationist, one of the most respected in the province, still active in the community at 79. Soft-spoken and gentle, he is still a farmer: he grows wheat and oats, albeit on a small patch – 32 hectares planted this year. His grandfather was a farmer too, on a property two kilometres east, where Scott grew up. Letting more than a quarter of his farm grow wild is a radical act. Scott wouldn’t say so. He does it “for nature,” he says, to protect the life that’s disappearing, from insects to owls to moose. The day before we met, he saw two yearling moose, as well as a whitetail doe with a fawn and a mule deer. There are bluebird nesting boxes all over the property. What makes all of this radical is the context. Modern agriculture is a high-tech, data-driven industry that uses autonomous field equipment that relies on AI, drones and satellite imagery to maximize resources – land – for profit. “Only a wild man could be so reckless as to let a valuable thing like land go free,” says Andrea Olive, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, a friend of Scott’s and the author of Protecting the Prairies: Lorne Scott and the Politics of Conservation . “It must bother his neighbours, who only see cash crops where Lorne sees true growth.” It does, and some have asked, politely, to rent those perfectly good hectares of his, to plow them under, get things going as God and the commodities markets intended. He tells them no, that their equipment is too big, “and they shake their heads and walk away.” There’s a sign at the entrance to his farm that says, “This Property Is Forever Protected.” That means there’s a conservation easement on part of the property to preserve its natural state. Scott still owns the land and can pass it to his children or whoever he wants, but the restrictions on development are permanent. Scott knows about easements: he served as Saskatchewan’s minister of environment and resource management for four years in the late ‘90s, in Roy Romanow’s NDP government, and was responsible for the Conservation Easements Act, aimed at restricting development of wild land on private property. Under the act, the farmer still owns the land but enters into an agreement with a non-profit, like Ducks Unlimited, to keep it wild, as, say, wetland or grassland. There are thousands of hectares under easement in Saskatchewan. Some ranchers find them useful for protecting natural grasslands for grazing. Grazing is good for grasslands. It disturbs the plants (as does wildfire) in ways that help them grow. A conservative estimate is that 80 per cent of the grassland in Saskatchewan has been lost since commercial agriculture began, most recently through the sale of Crown lands after Ottawa dismantled the 74-year-old Prairie Farm Rehabilitation program in 2009. In the first 20 years of the 21st century, the average farm size increased by about 20 per cent, while the number of farms shrank by 23 per cent. Farms are getting bigger, land prices are rising, and while most farms are owned by the families that work them, one to two per cent are owned by investors and 2.4 per cent by large-scale private landowners. From Manitoba to the Cypress Hills, southern Saskatchewan was once grassland where bison grazed and First Nations hunted. It’s now mostly agricultural, and many farms are dotted with oil wells and pumpjacks, sometimes called “nodding donkeys.” To Scott and groups like the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation, a non-profit he used to head, the mixed grasslands and fescue prairie are home to more than 30 species at risk, including the greater sage-grouse, and are valuable for that fact alone. Ottawa and the private sector (including Mosaic, a potash mining company, and the Weston family, which backs Be Giant ) have donated millions of dollars to prairie habitat preservation. “Everything gets bigger and better, supposedly,” says Scott, a man of few words until he gets wound up. “The biggest impact I see is on the natural environment. The wetlands, the bush are being cleared, and with equipment and technology, everything is workable these days for growing canola or wheat, whatever, and it's really made a big impact on the natural environment, and consequently some bird species have declined by 90 per cent or more, and largely due to agriculture, intensive farming.” According to Environment and Climate Change Canada, burrowing owl numbers declined 90 per cent from 1990 to 2000, then another 64 per cent between 2005 and 2015. They are small, oddball birds with long legs for running that live underground in tunnels dug by badgers. There are now fewer than 800 pairs left in Saskatchewan and Alberta. “Out in the country and the wild west, I call it, anything goes as long as it benefits you,” Scott says. Scott is not a born politician. He’s not an ideologue. He ran for office as a New Democrat, but in the 1980s, he joined the Progressive Conservative Party.

He said the haze, hot weather and dust at construction sites added to the strain. Workers remind one another to drink water and look after their health. Workers who spend hours outdoors have fewer options to avoid polluted air when their jobs depend on being outside. Hexacon Construction has issued N95 masks and uses the 24-hour PSI and visibility to guide safety measures at its sites, said environmental, health and safety manager Cai Li Ling (transliterated), 48. The company shares advice through safety briefings, meetings, emails and WhatsApp messages. Workers who feel unwell, struggle to breathe or experience eye irritation are told to seek help from the site safety team. Cai said the company would pause work whenever visibility was affected, regardless of the PSI reading, until conditions stabilised. UOB has also distributed masks and encouraged staff to limit outdoor activities. sources.evidenceText: SHENYANG, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity. The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail. The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming. Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus. The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure. The bones in its throat are similar to those of modern mammals, suggesting that behaviors such as swallowing, lapping and suckling may have already existed in the early ancestors of mammals, long before modern mammal groups appeared. "Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China. The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct. 7. ■
